The four-octave instrument sounds roughly from C4 to C8, an octave above what is written; there are also sizes from three to five and a half octaves. Four- and five-octave models usually sustain or damp the sound with a damper pedal, while the three-octave table model has none. The overall volume is weak, not enough to carry a full ensemble, and the instrument is mostly used to reinforce a melodic line or in chamber music.

The celesta is a keyboard-operated struck idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 111.222. It looks like a small upright piano; the keys drive small felt-covered hammers that strike metal bars hung over wooden resonators, producing a soft, bell-like timbre. It belongs to the percussion family, but in the orchestra it is usually counted in the keyboard section and played by a keyboard player, and it is commonly used in orchestral music, chamber music, opera and pop and jazz recordings to reinforce a melodic line or to play a solo passage.
